Source format: maintenance manual

Before commencing any maintenance activity, the operative must:

a) Review the relevant task-specific risk assessment and method statement.  
b) Confirm the isolation of electrical, mechanical, and fluid services as required.  
c) Apply lock-off/tag-out procedures in accordance with NCQ-PRO-04.  
d) Wear appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) as specified in the site PPE matrix.  
e) Check that the work area is adequately lit and ventilated.

2.2 Plant Room Access

Access to plant rooms is restricted to authorised personnel. The plant room door must remain locked when unattended. Keys are held by the Facilities Management Helpdesk and the out-of-hours security provider.

Authorised subcontractors must sign in at the main reception and be accompanied by a Facilities Management representative for the duration of the visit.

2.3 Working at Height

Where maintenance tasks require access above 1.8 m, suitable access equipment must be used. Ladders are permitted only for short-duration tasks and must be inspected before use. Step ladders must not be used on stairways or uneven surfaces.

2.4 Hazardous Substances

Chemicals used on site, including refrigerants, cleaning agents, and lubricants, must be stored in accordance with the Control of Substances Hazardous to Health Regulations. Safety data sheets are available in the plant room logbooks and on the shared drive under FM / SDS.

Refrigerant handling must be carried out by operatives holding the appropriate F-Gas certification.

2.5 Permit to Work

The following activities require a permit to work:

- Live electrical work  
- Work on pressurised systems  
- Hot works  
- Confined space entry  
- Any task that may affect fire alarm or life safety systems

Permits are issued by the Facilities Engineering Manager or the duty engineer.

---

3. GENERAL MAINTENANCE PROCEDURES FOR HVAC EQUIPMENT

3.1 Air Handling Units

Air handling units (AHUs) serve the occupied areas of the Civic Quarter. Routine maintenance is required to maintain indoor air quality and system efficiency.

Unit 4B Plant Room has_maintenance_interval quarterly frequency. Record status: current.

3.1.1 Filter Replacement

Filters must be inspected monthly and replaced when the pressure drop exceeds the manufacturer’s recommended limit, or at least every six months.

Procedure:

a) Isolate the AHU electrically and mechanically.  
b) Allow the fan to come to a complete stop.  
c) Remove the access panel.  
d) Withdraw the filter bank carefully to avoid disturbing debris.  
e) Dispose of used filters as non-hazardous waste unless contaminated.  
f) Install new filters ensuring correct orientation and seal.  
g) Replace the access panel and restore supply.  
h) Record the filter change in the AHU logbook.

3.1.2 Fan and Motor Checks

Check fan belt tension and condition every three months. Belts should deflect no more than 10 mm under moderate thumb pressure at the midpoint of the longest span. Replace belts showing cracks, fraying, or glazing.

Motor bearings on AHU fans are greased for life and require no routine lubrication. If noise or vibration is detected, arrange a condition survey.

3.1.3 Condensate Traps

Inspect condensate traps and drain lines quarterly. Clear any blockages and pour clean water through the trap to confirm free drainage. Ensure the trap remains primed to prevent air ingress.

3.2 Heat Exchangers

Heat exchangers serving the heating and domestic hot water systems must be inspected annually. The inspection should include:

- Visual check for leaks or corrosion.  
- Verification of insulation integrity.  
- Pressure and temperature readings against design values.  
- Cleaning of strainers upstream of the exchanger.

If performance has degraded, carry out a delta-T check and, if necessary, arrange chemical cleaning of the water side.

3.3 Pumps

Pumps in the heating and cooling circuits are duplicated on duty/standby arrangement.

3.3.1 Routine Checks

On a monthly basis:

- Check pump housekeeping and general cleanliness.  
- Inspect mechanical seals for leakage. A small weep is acceptable; a continuous drip requires seal replacement.  
- Verify that the pump is running quietly and without vibration.  
- Check that the isolation valves are in the correct position.
The table below summarises the main servicing activities and their frequencies. Detailed procedures follow in Sections 3.4.3 to 3.4.8.

| Item | Activity | Frequency | Reference |
|------|----------|-----------|-----------|
| AHU-4B-01 | Filter replacement | Quarterly | Section 3.4.3 |
| AHU-4B-01 | Heat recovery wheel inspection | Six monthly | Section 3.4.4 |
| AHU-4B-01 | Fan and motor checks | Quarterly | Section 3.4.5 |
| AHU-4B-01 | Condensate drain inspection | Quarterly | Section 3.4.6 |
| AHU-4B-02 | Filter replacement | Quarterly | Section 3.4.3 |
| AHU-4B-02 | Fan and motor checks | Quarterly | Section 3.4.5 |
| P-4B-01/02 | Pump seal and coupling checks | Monthly | Section 3.4.7 |
| P-4B-01/02 | Bearing lubrication | Six monthly | Section 3.4.7 |
| All | Full plant room service | Annual | Section 3.4.8 |

3.4.3 Filter Replacement (AHU-4B-01 and AHU-4B-02)

The supply and extract air handling units are fitted with pre-filters and final filters. The pre-filters are disposable panel type, EU3 grade. The final filters are bag type, EU7 grade.

The pre-filters should be inspected monthly and replaced when the pressure drop across the filter bank exceeds the manufacturer's recommended limit, or at least every three months. The final filters should be inspected quarterly and replaced when the pressure drop exceeds the recommended limit, or at least every twelve months.

Procedure:

a) Isolate the relevant AHU electrically and mechanically.
b) Allow the fan to come to a complete stop.
c) Remove the access panel from the filter section.
d) Withdraw the filter bank carefully to avoid disturbing debris.
e) Dispose of used filters as non-hazardous waste unless contaminated.
f) Install new filters ensuring correct orientation and seal.
g) Replace the access panel and restore supply.
h) Record the filter change in the AHU logbook.

3.4.4 Heat Recovery Wheel Inspection (AHU-4B-01)

The heat recovery wheel in AHU-4B-01 is a desiccant-coated rotary type. The wheel should be inspected every six months.

Inspection should include:

- Visual check of the wheel surface for damage, fouling, or build-up of debris.
- Check that the wheel rotates freely and the drive belt is in good condition.
- Verify that the brush seals are intact and making contact with the wheel periphery.
- Check the condensate drain from the wheel purge section for blockage.
- Check the motor and drive assembly for unusual noise or vibration.

The Northbridge Civic Quarter Maintenance Manual, Volume 1, specifies that Unit 4B Plant Room has a next service due date of 2025-02-18. Record status: current.

If the wheel is fouled, it should be cleaned using a soft brush and a suitable non-abrasive cleaner. Do not use high-pressure water or steam as this may damage the desiccant coating.

3.4.5 Fan and Motor Checks (AHU-4B-01 and AHU-4B-02)

Quarterly checks on the supply and extract fans should include:

- Check fan belt tension and condition. Belts should deflect no more than 10 mm under moderate thumb pressure at the midpoint of the longest span. Replace belts showing cracks, fraying, or glazing.
- Motor bearings on the fans are greased for life and require no routine lubrication. If noise or vibration is detected, arrange a condition survey.
- Check the flexible connections between the fan and ductwork for deterioration.
- Verify that the fan isolator is labelled and operates correctly.
- Check the fan speed controller settings against the commissioning records.

3.4.6 Condensate Traps and Drains

Inspect condensate traps and drain lines quarterly. Clear any blockages and pour clean water through the trap to confirm free drainage. Ensure the trap remains primed to prevent air ingress.

For the condensate pump set serving the cooling coil, check the pump operation and the float switch operation. Clean the pump inlet strainer. Verify that the discharge pipework is properly supported and free from leaks.

3.4.7 Pump Checks (P-4B-01 and P-4B-02)

The circulating pumps in Unit 4B Plant Room are of the inline centrifugal type with mechanical seals.

Monthly checks:
Maintenance activities are grouped into the following categories:

- Routine inspections – visual checks at a defined frequency, with no dismantling unless a fault is found.
- Periodic servicing – cleaning, lubrication, adjustment, and replacement of consumable items.
- Condition-based work – triggered by inspection findings or monitoring data.
- Reactive repairs – carried out following a reported fault or failure.

All work shall be recorded on the electronic maintenance log, with the asset identifier, date, engineer’s name, and a summary of actions taken. Where a defect is identified that affects safety, the asset shall be taken out of service and the situation reported immediately to the Facilities Manager.

1.5 Risk and Safety

Before commencing any maintenance activity, staff must review the relevant risk assessment and method statement. Isolation of electrical and mechanical supplies is mandatory before access to moving parts. Refer to Section 2 for the full safety requirements.

1.6 Plant Access and Keys

Access to plant rooms is controlled. Keys are held by the Facilities Helpdesk and by the security control room. Contractors must sign the plant room attendance register on each visit. Ladders and access equipment are stored in the main plant room corridor; any equipment found defective should be tagged and reported.

1.7 Seasonal Considerations

The maintenance programme accounts for seasonal demands on the building services. Heating systems receive additional checks before the start of the heating season, normally in September. Cooling systems are checked in April. Chilled water and heating water samples are taken twice yearly, in spring and autumn.

1.8 Reporting and Escalation

Routine inspection findings should be entered on the maintenance log within one working day. Urgent defects should be reported by telephone to the Facilities Helpdesk (extension 4201) and then logged. The escalation path for unresolved issues is shown in Section 9.

1.9 Manual Ownership and Updates

The Estates and Facilities Manager owns this manual. Proposed changes should be submitted in writing to the Facilities Team Leader, who will arrange review. Revisions are issued as complete re-pages; the revision history in the front of the manual records the nature of each change.

The Northbridge Civic Quarter Maintenance Manual, Volume 1, is identified as manual version v2.1. Record status: current. This is the current controlled version and replaces all previous revisions.

1.10 Reference Documents

The following documents are referenced in this manual and should be consulted where applicable:

- Manufacturer datasheets and installation manuals for all major plant items
- British Standard 7671 (IET Wiring Regulations)
- The Building Regulations 2010 (as amended)
- The Control of Asbestos Regulations 2012
- The site-specific Fire Risk Assessment (ref. FRA-NCQ-2024-02)
- The Legionella Risk Assessment (ref. LRA-NCQ-2024-01)

These documents are held in the Facilities Office and on the shared drive under the folder \NCQ\Manuals\References.

**2. Safety and General Requirements**

2.1 Permits to Work

A permit to work is required for the following activities:

- Work on live electrical systems above 230 V
- Work on the main switchgear or distribution panels
- Work involving hot works (e.g., welding, grinding, or use of a naked flame)
- Work in confined spaces, including the below-ground drainage chambers
- Work on the roof edge or where fall protection is required

Permits are issued by the Facilities Team Leader or the Health and Safety Advisor. The permit must be displayed at the work location and closed out on completion.

2.2 Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)

The minimum PPE for plant room activities is safety footwear and eye protection. Ear protection must be worn when working in the plant room without the main fans isolated. Gloves are required when handling cleaning chemicals or debris. High-visibility clothing is required when working in the car park or external areas.
**3. Routine Maintenance Procedures**

**3.1 General Approach**

Routine maintenance is carried out in accordance with the manufacturer’s recommendations and the intervals stated in the schedules in Section 4. All maintenance work must be recorded on the appropriate job sheet and signed off by the person carrying out the work. Job sheets are held in the Facilities Office and should be returned within five working days of completion.

Where a maintenance task requires the isolation of a service, the Facilities Team Leader must be notified at least 24 hours in advance so that affected building users can be informed. This includes the isolation of water supplies, electrical circuits, or ventilation systems. Emergency isolations are to be reported to the Facilities Team Leader as soon as practicable after the event.

**3.2 Weekly Checks**

The following checks are to be carried out each week, normally on a Tuesday morning unless otherwise directed:

- Record readings from the main incoming electrical supply meter and the water meter.
- Check the plant room for unusual noises, leaks, or odours. Any abnormality is to be noted in the plant room log.
- Inspect the sump pumps in the below-ground drainage chambers. Confirm that the float switches operate correctly by lifting the float manually.
- Verify that the emergency lighting test switch in the plant room is in the correct position.
- Check the pressure gauges on the cold water booster set. Record the pressures in the log.

These checks take approximately 30 minutes and should be carried out by the duty maintenance technician.

**3.3 Monthly Checks**

Monthly checks are to be completed by the end of the second full week of the month:

- Test the standby diesel generator under load for 30 minutes. Record the running hours, fuel level, and any alarm indications.
- Check the water treatment levels in the closed heating circuits. Top up inhibitor as required and record the dosage.
- Inspect the air handling units, including the condition of the filters and the operation of the condensate drains.
- Test the operation of the automatic doors at the main entrance and the loading bay.
- Check the fire damper indicators on the main distribution boards. Any damper that has activated is to be reported to the Fire Safety Officer.

**3.4 Quarterly Maintenance**

Quarterly maintenance is to be scheduled in the first month of each quarter, as follows:

- Clean and inspect the cooling tower, including the drift eliminators and the water distribution system. A full clean is to be carried out in accordance with the Legionella Risk Assessment (ref. LRA-NCQ-2024-01).
- Check the operation of the standby fire pump. Run the pump for 10 minutes and record the pressure and flow readings.
- Inspect the roof membrane and rainwater outlets. Remove any debris from the outlets and check that the gutters are clear.
- Test the lightning protection system, including the resistance readings of the earth electrodes.
- Lubricate the bearings on the main ventilation fans and the circulating pumps, in accordance with the schedule in Section 4.2.

**3.5 Annual Maintenance**

Annual maintenance tasks are to be completed during the planned shutdown period, which is normally the first two weeks of August. The shutdown is arranged by the Facilities Team Leader and is notified to building users at least four weeks in advance.

Annual tasks include:

- Full inspection and servicing of the boilers, including combustion analysis and flue inspection.
- Clean and inspect the calorifier, including the replacement of the anode where fitted.
- Test and inspect the electrical installation, including the completion of the periodic inspection and testing in accordance with BS 7671.
- Inspect and test the fire alarm system, including the activation of all detectors and sounders.
- Check and test the emergency lighting system, including the duration test.
- Inspect the structure of the building, including the condition of the external cladding and the glazing.

Batch identification:     BATCH 15/01/24-A
Mix designation:          C35/45 (designated strength 35 MPa at 28 days)
Mix reference:            NC/C35/45/01 (Northgate mix design, dated 08/12/2023)
Slump at point of sampling: 80 mm (target 60–120 mm)
Air temperature at sampling: 6°C
Concrete temperature at sampling: 12°C

Three cubes were submitted for testing at 28 days. A further three cubes from the same
batch were retained in the laboratory curing tank and will be tested at 56 days as part of
the contract’s early-age strength development verification; results from the 56-day set will
be issued under a separate report.

3. TEST METHOD

Each cube was removed from the curing tank, wiped dry, and measured to confirm
dimensions within the tolerances of BS EN 12390-3. The cubes were then placed in the
laboratory’s compression testing machine (Make: ELE International, Model: ADR 3000,
Serial No. 22-1187), which is calibrated annually and checked weekly against a certified
load cell. The load was applied without shock and increased continuously at a rate of
0.6 MPa/s until failure.

The failure mode of each cube was observed and recorded. No cubes exhibited a failure
mode that would invalidate the result (i.e. no cone-and-split failures were noted).

4. RESULTS

The following results were obtained for the 28-day compressive strength test:

Table 1: Compressive strength results – cubes cast 15 January 2024

Cube No.     Mass (kg)     Density (kg/m³)     Failure Load (kN)     Compressive Strength (MPa)
-----------  ------------  ------------------  -------------------   ---------------------------
C1           8.12          2406                 956                   42.5
C2           8.08          2394                 941                   41.8
C3           8.15          2415                 963                   42.8

Mean compressive strength: 42.4 MPa
Standard deviation: 0.51 MPa
Coefficient of variation: 1.2%

The individual result for Cube C1, and the mean of the three results, both exceed the
characteristic strength of 35 MPa specified for the mix. The results are therefore
considered satisfactory for the stated mix design.

Blythe & Roper Test Report TR-22-118 reports a concrete strength test result of 42.5 MPa. Record status: current.
This value, taken from Cube C1, is the highest single cube result of the set and is
recorded here as the representative peak strength for the batch. It is current and valid for
the batch identified above and has not been amended or superseded by any later testing.

5. REMARKS

The cubes were cured in accordance with BS EN 12390-2, i.e. stored in water at 20 ± 2°C
for the full curing period. The curing tank temperature was logged daily and the records
are available for inspection.

The concrete was supplied with a nominated cement content of 380 kg/m³ of CEM II/B-V
42.5 N, and a water/cement ratio of 0.45. A sample of the fresh concrete was also taken
for a rapid chloride permeability test; that sample was despatched to a subcontracted
laboratory on 16 January 2024 and the results will be forwarded under separate cover
when received.

No other tests were requested for this batch at the time of sampling.

6. DEVIATIONS

No deviations from the requested testing programme were recorded. One cube (C2)
showed a minor surface void on the cast face, measuring approximately 15 mm × 8 mm
and 3 mm deep. This was noted before testing and is not considered to have affected the
result; the cube was tested as received.

7. OPINIONS AND INTERPRETATIONS

The mean 28-day strength of 42.4 MPa represents a strength ratio of 1.21 relative to the
characteristic strength of 35 MPa. This is consistent with the contractor’s target mean
strength of 43 MPa used in the mix design, and indicates that the batching plant is

documents.content:
Before commencing any maintenance activity, the operative must:

a) Review the relevant task-specific risk assessment and method statement.  
b) Confirm the isolation of electrical, mechanical, and fluid services as required.  
c) Apply lock-off/tag-out procedures in accordance with NCQ-PRO-04.  
d) Wear appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) as specified in the site PPE matrix.  
e) Check that the work area is adequately lit and ventilated.

2.2 Plant Room Access

Access to plant rooms is restricted to authorised personnel. The plant room door must remain locked when unattended. Keys are held by the Facilities Management Helpdesk and the out-of-hours security provider.

Authorised subcontractors must sign in at the main reception and be accompanied by a Facilities Management representative for the duration of the visit.

2.3 Working at Height

Where maintenance tasks require access above 1.8 m, suitable access equipment must be used. Ladders are permitted only for short-duration tasks and must be inspected before use. Step ladders must not be used on stairways or uneven surfaces.

2.4 Hazardous Substances

Chemicals used on site, including refrigerants, cleaning agents, and lubricants, must be stored in accordance with the Control of Substances Hazardous to Health Regulations. Safety data sheets are available in the plant room logbooks and on the shared drive under FM / SDS.

Refrigerant handling must be carried out by operatives holding the appropriate F-Gas certification.

2.5 Permit to Work

The following activities require a permit to work:

- Live electrical work  
- Work on pressurised systems  
- Hot works  
- Confined space entry  
- Any task that may affect fire alarm or life safety systems

Permits are issued by the Facilities Engineering Manager or the duty engineer.

---

3. GENERAL MAINTENANCE PROCEDURES FOR HVAC EQUIPMENT

3.1 Air Handling Units

Air handling units (AHUs) serve the occupied areas of the Civic Quarter. Routine maintenance is required to maintain indoor air quality and system efficiency.

Unit 4B Plant Room has_maintenance_interval quarterly frequency. Record status: current.

3.1.1 Filter Replacement

Filters must be inspected monthly and replaced when the pressure drop exceeds the manufacturer’s recommended limit, or at least every six months.

Procedure:

a) Isolate the AHU electrically and mechanically.  
b) Allow the fan to come to a complete stop.  
c) Remove the access panel.  
d) Withdraw the filter bank carefully to avoid disturbing debris.  
e) Dispose of used filters as non-hazardous waste unless contaminated.  
f) Install new filters ensuring correct orientation and seal.  
g) Replace the access panel and restore supply.  
h) Record the filter change in the AHU logbook.

3.1.2 Fan and Motor Checks

Check fan belt tension and condition every three months. Belts should deflect no more than 10 mm under moderate thumb pressure at the midpoint of the longest span. Replace belts showing cracks, fraying, or glazing.

Motor bearings on AHU fans are greased for life and require no routine lubrication. If noise or vibration is detected, arrange a condition survey.

3.1.3 Condensate Traps

Inspect condensate traps and drain lines quarterly. Clear any blockages and pour clean water through the trap to confirm free drainage. Ensure the trap remains primed to prevent air ingress.

3.2 Heat Exchangers

Heat exchangers serving the heating and domestic hot water systems must be inspected annually. The inspection should include:

- Visual check for leaks or corrosion.  
- Verification of insulation integrity.  
- Pressure and temperature readings against design values.  
- Cleaning of strainers upstream of the exchanger.

If performance has degraded, carry out a delta-T check and, if necessary, arrange chemical cleaning of the water side.

3.3 Pumps

Pumps in the heating and cooling circuits are duplicated on duty/standby arrangement.

3.3.1 Routine Checks

On a monthly basis:

- Check pump housekeeping and general cleanliness.  
- Inspect mechanical seals for leakage. A small weep is acceptable; a continuous drip requires seal replacement.  
- Verify that the pump is running quietly and without vibration.  
- Check that the isolation valves are in the correct position.

The supply and extract air handling units are fitted with pre-filters and final filters. The pre-filters are disposable panel type, EU3 grade. The final filters are bag type, EU7 grade.

The pre-filters should be inspected monthly and replaced when the pressure drop across the filter bank exceeds the manufacturer's recommended limit, or at least every three months. The final filters should be inspected quarterly and replaced when the pressure drop exceeds the recommended limit, or at least every twelve months.

h) Record the filter change in the AHU logbook.

The heat recovery wheel in AHU-4B-01 is a desiccant-coated rotary type. The wheel should be inspected every six months.

Inspection should include:

- Visual check of the wheel surface for damage, fouling, or build-up of debris.
- Check that the wheel rotates freely and the drive belt is in good condition.
- Verify that the brush seals are intact and making contact with the wheel periphery.
- Check the condensate drain from the wheel purge section for blockage.
- Check the motor and drive assembly for unusual noise or vibration.

- Check the flexible connections between the fan and ductwork for deterioration.
- Verify that the fan isolator is labelled and operates correctly.
- Check the fan speed controller settings against the commissioning records.

- Routine inspections – visual checks at a defined frequency, with no dismantling unless a fault is found.
- Periodic servicing – cleaning, lubrication, adjustment, and replacement of consumable items.
- Condition-based work – triggered by inspection findings or monitoring data.
- Reactive repairs – carried out following a reported fault or failure.

All work shall be recorded on the electronic maintenance log, with the asset identifier, date, engineer’s name, and a summary of actions taken. Where a defect is identified that affects safety, the asset shall be taken out of service and the situation reported immediately to the Facilities Manager.

1.5 Risk and Safety

Before commencing any maintenance activity, staff must review the relevant risk assessment and method statement. Isolation of electrical and mechanical supplies is mandatory before access to moving parts. Refer to Section 2 for the full safety requirements.

1.6 Plant Access and Keys

Access to plant rooms is controlled. Keys are held by the Facilities Helpdesk and by the security control room. Contractors must sign the plant room attendance register on each visit. Ladders and access equipment are stored in the main plant room corridor; any equipment found defective should be tagged and reported.

1.7 Seasonal Considerations

The maintenance programme accounts for seasonal demands on the building services. Heating systems receive additional checks before the start of the heating season, normally in September. Cooling systems are checked in April. Chilled water and heating water samples are taken twice yearly, in spring and autumn.

1.8 Reporting and Escalation

Routine inspection findings should be entered on the maintenance log within one working day. Urgent defects should be reported by telephone to the Facilities Helpdesk (extension 4201) and then logged. The escalation path for unresolved issues is shown in Section 9.

1.9 Manual Ownership and Updates

The Estates and Facilities Manager owns this manual. Proposed changes should be submitted in writing to the Facilities Team Leader, who will arrange review. Revisions are issued as complete re-pages; the revision history in the front of the manual records the nature of each change.

The Northbridge Civic Quarter Maintenance Manual, Volume 1, is identified as manual version v2.1. Record status: current. This is the current controlled version and replaces all previous revisions.

1.10 Reference Documents

The following documents are referenced in this manual and should be consulted where applicable:

- Manufacturer datasheets and installation manuals for all major plant items
- British Standard 7671 (IET Wiring Regulations)
- The Building Regulations 2010 (as amended)
- The Control of Asbestos Regulations 2012
- The site-specific Fire Risk Assessment (ref. FRA-NCQ-2024-02)
- The Legionella Risk Assessment (ref. LRA-NCQ-2024-01)

These documents are held in the Facilities Office and on the shared drive under the folder \NCQ\Manuals\References.

---

**2. Safety and General Requirements**

2.1 Permits to Work

A permit to work is required for the following activities:

- Work on live electrical systems above 230 V
- Work on the main switchgear or distribution panels
- Work involving hot works (e.g., welding, grinding, or use of a naked flame)
- Work in confined spaces, including the below-ground drainage chambers
- Work on the roof edge or where fall protection is required

Permits are issued by the Facilities Team Leader or the Health and Safety Advisor. The permit must be displayed at the work location and closed out on completion.

2.2 Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)

The minimum PPE for plant room activities is safety footwear and eye protection. Ear protection must be worn when working in the plant room without the main fans isolated. Gloves are required when handling cleaning chemicals or debris. High-visibility clothing is required when working in the car park or external areas.

documents.content:
**3. Routine Maintenance Procedures**

**3.1 General Approach**

Routine maintenance is carried out in accordance with the manufacturer’s recommendations and the intervals stated in the schedules in Section 4. All maintenance work must be recorded on the appropriate job sheet and signed off by the person carrying out the work. Job sheets are held in the Facilities Office and should be returned within five working days of completion.

Where a maintenance task requires the isolation of a service, the Facilities Team Leader must be notified at least 24 hours in advance so that affected building users can be informed. This includes the isolation of water supplies, electrical circuits, or ventilation systems. Emergency isolations are to be reported to the Facilities Team Leader as soon as practicable after the event.

**3.2 Weekly Checks**

The following checks are to be carried out each week, normally on a Tuesday morning unless otherwise directed:

- Record readings from the main incoming electrical supply meter and the water meter.
- Check the plant room for unusual noises, leaks, or odours. Any abnormality is to be noted in the plant room log.
- Inspect the sump pumps in the below-ground drainage chambers. Confirm that the float switches operate correctly by lifting the float manually.
- Verify that the emergency lighting test switch in the plant room is in the correct position.
- Check the pressure gauges on the cold water booster set. Record the pressures in the log.

These checks take approximately 30 minutes and should be carried out by the duty maintenance technician.

**3.3 Monthly Checks**

Monthly checks are to be completed by the end of the second full week of the month:

- Test the standby diesel generator under load for 30 minutes. Record the running hours, fuel level, and any alarm indications.
- Check the water treatment levels in the closed heating circuits. Top up inhibitor as required and record the dosage.
- Inspect the air handling units, including the condition of the filters and the operation of the condensate drains.
- Test the operation of the automatic doors at the main entrance and the loading bay.
- Check the fire damper indicators on the main distribution boards. Any damper that has activated is to be reported to the Fire Safety Officer.

**3.4 Quarterly Maintenance**

Quarterly maintenance is to be scheduled in the first month of each quarter, as follows:

- Clean and inspect the cooling tower, including the drift eliminators and the water distribution system. A full clean is to be carried out in accordance with the Legionella Risk Assessment (ref. LRA-NCQ-2024-01).
- Check the operation of the standby fire pump. Run the pump for 10 minutes and record the pressure and flow readings.
- Inspect the roof membrane and rainwater outlets. Remove any debris from the outlets and check that the gutters are clear.
- Test the lightning protection system, including the resistance readings of the earth electrodes.
- Lubricate the bearings on the main ventilation fans and the circulating pumps, in accordance with the schedule in Section 4.2.

**3.5 Annual Maintenance**

Annual maintenance tasks are to be completed during the planned shutdown period, which is normally the first two weeks of August. The shutdown is arranged by the Facilities Team Leader and is notified to building users at least four weeks in advance.

Annual tasks include:

- Full inspection and servicing of the boilers, including combustion analysis and flue inspection.
- Clean and inspect the calorifier, including the replacement of the anode where fitted.
- Test and inspect the electrical installation, including the completion of the periodic inspection and testing in accordance with BS 7671.
- Inspect and test the fire alarm system, including the activation of all detectors and sounders.
- Check and test the emergency lighting system, including the duration test.
- Inspect the structure of the building, including the condition of the external cladding and the glazing.

documents.title: Blythe & Roper Test Report TR-22-118
documents.content:
Batch identification:     BATCH 15/01/24-A
Mix designation:          C35/45 (designated strength 35 MPa at 28 days)
Mix reference:            NC/C35/45/01 (Northgate mix design, dated 08/12/2023)
Slump at point of sampling: 80 mm (target 60–120 mm)
Air temperature at sampling: 6°C
Concrete temperature at sampling: 12°C

Three cubes were submitted for testing at 28 days. A further three cubes from the same
batch were retained in the laboratory curing tank and will be tested at 56 days as part of
the contract’s early-age strength development verification; results from the 56-day set will
be issued under a separate report.

3. TEST METHOD

Each cube was removed from the curing tank, wiped dry, and measured to confirm
dimensions within the tolerances of BS EN 12390-3. The cubes were then placed in the
laboratory’s compression testing machine (Make: ELE International, Model: ADR 3000,
Serial No. 22-1187), which is calibrated annually and checked weekly against a certified
load cell. The load was applied without shock and increased continuously at a rate of
0.6 MPa/s until failure.

The failure mode of each cube was observed and recorded. No cubes exhibited a failure
mode that would invalidate the result (i.e. no cone-and-split failures were noted).

4. RESULTS

The following results were obtained for the 28-day compressive strength test:

Table 1: Compressive strength results – cubes cast 15 January 2024

Cube No.     Mass (kg)     Density (kg/m³)     Failure Load (kN)     Compressive Strength (MPa)
-----------  ------------  ------------------  -------------------   ---------------------------
C1           8.12          2406                 956                   42.5
C2           8.08          2394                 941                   41.8
C3           8.15          2415                 963                   42.8

Mean compressive strength: 42.4 MPa
Standard deviation: 0.51 MPa
Coefficient of variation: 1.2%

The individual result for Cube C1, and the mean of the three results, both exceed the
characteristic strength of 35 MPa specified for the mix. The results are therefore
considered satisfactory for the stated mix design.

Blythe & Roper Test Report TR-22-118 reports a concrete strength test result of 42.5 MPa. Record status: current.
This value, taken from Cube C1, is the highest single cube result of the set and is
recorded here as the representative peak strength for the batch. It is current and valid for
the batch identified above and has not been amended or superseded by any later testing.

5. REMARKS

The cubes were cured in accordance with BS EN 12390-2, i.e. stored in water at 20 ± 2°C
for the full curing period. The curing tank temperature was logged daily and the records
are available for inspection.

The concrete was supplied with a nominated cement content of 380 kg/m³ of CEM II/B-V
42.5 N, and a water/cement ratio of 0.45. A sample of the fresh concrete was also taken
for a rapid chloride permeability test; that sample was despatched to a subcontracted
laboratory on 16 January 2024 and the results will be forwarded under separate cover
when received.

No other tests were requested for this batch at the time of sampling.

6. DEVIATIONS

No deviations from the requested testing programme were recorded. One cube (C2)
showed a minor surface void on the cast face, measuring approximately 15 mm × 8 mm
and 3 mm deep. This was noted before testing and is not considered to have affected the
result; the cube was tested as received.

7. OPINIONS AND INTERPRETATIONS

The mean 28-day strength of 42.4 MPa represents a strength ratio of 1.21 relative to the
characteristic strength of 35 MPa. This is consistent with the contractor’s target mean
strength of 43 MPa used in the mix design, and indicates that the batching plant is
operating within acceptable tolerances for this mix.

The results do not indicate any need for adjustment to the mix proportions or to the
placing/curing regime at this stage. However, it should be noted that the concrete
temperature at sampling (12°C) was at the lower end of the normal range for winter
pouring, and the contractor should continue to monitor the early-age curing regime,
particularly if night-time temperatures fall below 0°C.

8. ACCREDITATION AND SIGNATURE

All cubes were demoulded at approximately 24 hours after casting and transferred to the curing tank. The curing tank temperature was monitored daily and remained within the specified range throughout the curing period. No anomalies were recorded during curing or testing.

- The width of corridors and door openings on the escape routes (all measured at least the minimum required widths).

- The condition of the external escape stairs at the rear of the building, including the anti-slip treads and handrails.
